title: Teaching a model to read addresses out of free-form text
question: Tell me about a time you had to learn an entirely new domain.

situation: I spent one day a week for a year working with the company's R&D innovation lab, exploring how emerging technologies could automate manual, text-heavy operations.

I had little previous experience in machine learning or natural language processing, but one of the problems we wanted to explore was whether free-form operational text could be turned into structured data automatically.
task: I took ownership of building a prototype that could extract the individual components of physical addresses from unstructured text, including messy real-world inputs that did not follow a consistent format.
action: I started by learning the problem space rather than immediately choosing a technology. I spoke with computer science professors at ULB and investigated whether we should build a neural network ourselves using TensorFlow or use an existing NLP framework.

Given that I only had one day a week for the project, I eventually chose spaCy in Python because it provided a strong pre-trained neural-network foundation and let me spend more of the available time on the actual data and problem rather than infrastructure.
I then built the training pipeline, curated and cleaned the datasets, experimented with different features and model configurations, and iterated against real-world address examples.

I also built a custom validation tool around the model. It generated interactive HTML reports showing accuracy, performance and failed cases, with misclassified fields highlighted so we could quickly distinguish problems in the source data from weaknesses in the model.
result: I delivered a working NLP prototype and validation framework that demonstrated that free-form operational text could be transformed into structured address data with useful accuracy.
The work was selected for presentation at the Swift Operations Forum in Amsterdam, where we presented both the results and the methodology behind the prototype.

challenge: The biggest challenge was making meaningful progress with only one day a week while starting from a relatively unfamiliar technical domain. I had to balance learning the underlying machine-learning concepts with making practical progress, which meant being willing to abandon a technically interesting approach when it was not the right fit for the available time.
hardestBug: A surprisingly difficult preprocessing problem was deciding whether consecutive lines in a free-form text block represented separate address fields or were actually parts of the same logical field. I built structural pattern matching around the expected output schema and used the resulting validation feedback to improve the preprocessing and model behaviour.
differently: I would establish clearer success criteria and a representative evaluation dataset earlier. That would have made it easier to compare approaches objectively and decide sooner which experiments were worth pursuing within the limited time available.
aboutYourself: The project showed me that I am comfortable entering a domain where I am not yet an expert and becoming productive through self-directed learning. I also learned that I enjoy the combination of research and engineering: understanding a new concept, questioning the available approaches, and turning it into something practical.
enjoyed: I particularly enjoyed building the validation tool. Turning model output into an interactive report with accuracy summaries, graphs and highlighted failures made the experimentation much more tangible and gave us a fast way to understand why the model was getting cases wrong.
